newsitem.title: CHINA: Chinese, British officials begin Beijing talks.
newsitem.headline: Chinese, British officials begin Beijing talks.

text.p: With less than one year to go before the British colony of Hong Kong returns to Beijing's rule, Chinese and British officials began talks on Tuesday to iron out remaining differences, and said they expected progress.

"We have reason to expect that this plenary session will produce more progress," the Xinhua news agency quoted Chinese senior representative Zhao Jihua as saying at the start of the three days of talks.

Sources close to the 37th meeting of the Sino-British Joint Liaison Group, whose task is to hammer out issues that must be resolved before Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30, 1997, said progress was possible in several areas.

With relations improving between Britain and China in recent months, the sources said agreement was possible on the fraught issue of whether to hold a joint handover ceremony as well as a dispute over a much-needed ninth shipping container terminal.

"Bilateral relations are now developing towards the direction of further improvement," Xinhua news agency quoted Zhao as saying as the meeting got under way in Beijing, adding that the improvement had resulted from bilateral contacts since the previous meeting.
Britain's chief delegate, Hugh Davies, said he, too, hoped for progress and made a light-hearted reference toward gaining results before China's mid-autumn Moon Festival on September 27.
"It is certainly our intention to live up to the spirit of the Moon Festival and produce the next sound harvest on its occasion," Xinhua quoted Davies as saying.
Although the handover is only 287 days away, several contentious issues remain including the handover ceremony, the future of democracy and human rights, and infrastructure projects.

The meeting was expected to discuss issues such as concluding the transfer of political power in Hong Kong, its future participation in international organisations and treaties and the localisation of Hong Kong laws and tourist documents.
The group was still confronted with "very arduous" tasks, Zhao said, adding that China hoped for breakthroughs in the current round.
